titleEn: Contend, LORD, with those who contend with me
progression: | Dm Dm | Gm Gm | Dm A | Dm Dm |
intro: Twenty-eight verses of a man asking to be defended in court and in the field at the same time. It is one of the harshest psalms in the book: it asks for the attackers to be shamed, tripped, and caught in their own net, and it never softens that. It is not part of the fixed daily service; it belongs to the monthly cycle that reads the whole book, and to the custom of saying Tehillim for someone in trouble. For a learner it is a grammar drill. Almost every enemy is a participle used as a noun (those who fight me, those who seek my life, those who plot my harm), and almost every request is a jussive, the short third-person form that means let them be.

stichs.en: Of David.
Contend, LORD, with those who contend with me;
fight against those who fight me.

verses.summary: The psalm opens as a lawsuit and a battle in the same breath: one verb for pleading a case, one for making war. Nothing has been described yet, only demanded.

stichs.en: Take hold of shield and buckler,
and rise up as my help.

verses.summary: God is asked to arm Himself. Two different words for shield, a small one and a body-length one, and then a verb of standing up.

stichs.en: Draw out the spear and close the way against my pursuers;
say to my soul: I am your salvation.

verses.summary: The weapons turn into an order to speak. What the speaker actually wants is four words long, and it is said to his own soul rather than to the enemy.

stichs.en: Let those who seek my life be shamed and humiliated;
let those who plot my harm be turned back and disgraced.

verses.summary: The first of three curses on the attackers. They are named only by what they do, seeking a life and plotting harm, never by a name of their own.

stichs.en: Let them be like chaff before the wind,
with the angel of the LORD driving them.

verses.summary: The wish turns into an image. Chaff has no weight of its own, and the wind here is given a driver.

stichs.en: Let their way be dark and slippery,
with the angel of the LORD pursuing them.

verses.summary: The pair completes verse 5: dark and slippery underfoot, with the same angel now behind them rather than in front.

stichs.en: For without cause they hid their net over a pit for me,
without cause they dug it for my life.

verses.summary: The reason arrives after the curse, and it is said twice in one verse: without cause. The pit and the net are hunting equipment being used on a man.

stichs.en: Let ruin come upon him before he knows it,
and let the net he hid catch him;
let him fall into it, into the ruin.

verses.summary: The punishment asked for is the trap itself. Three clauses, each one turning the hunter's own gear back on him, with the word for ruin framing both ends.

stichs.en: And my soul will rejoice in the LORD,
it will delight in His salvation.

verses.summary: The first turn to praise, and the first quiet verse. Two verbs of rejoicing stand where the enemy had two verbs of hunting.

stichs.en: All my bones will say: LORD,
who is like You, rescuing the poor from one stronger than he,
the poor and the needy from the one who robs him?

verses.summary: Praise from the skeleton outward. The question who is like You is answered not by power in the abstract but by one specific act, taking the weak out of a stronger hand.

stichs.en: Witnesses of violence rise up;
they ask me about what I do not know.

verses.summary: The scene becomes a courtroom. Witnesses of violence is a legal phrase, and the charge is that they question him about things he has no knowledge of.

stichs.en: They repay me evil in place of good;
bereavement to my soul.

verses.summary: The exchange rate of the psalm: evil handed back for good. The last two words drop the argument and simply state the cost.

stichs.en: But as for me, when they were sick my clothing was sackcloth,
I afflicted my soul with fasting,
and my prayer would return upon my own bosom.

verses.summary: The counter-testimony, and the longest verse so far. He fasted for the people now hunting him, and the last clause leaves it open where that prayer ended up.

stichs.en: I went about as though for a friend, for a brother of mine;
like one mourning a mother I bowed down in black.

verses.summary: The mourning is spelled out in family terms. A friend, a brother, a mother: three degrees of closeness, none of them owed to these people.

stichs.en: But at my stumbling they rejoiced and gathered;
they gathered against me, attackers I did not know;
they tore at me and would not stop.

verses.summary: The reversal, stated plainly. He mourned when they were sick; they assembled when he stumbled. Two verbs of tearing and of not stopping close the verse.

stichs.en: With the profane, who mock for a cake,
they gnashed their teeth at me.

verses.summary: The most obscure verse in the psalm. Whatever the middle words mean exactly, the picture is mockery around a table, and teeth.

stichs.en: My Lord, how long will You look on?
Bring my soul back from their ravages,
my only one from the young lions.

verses.summary: The first direct address since verse 3, and the first how long. My only one is a name for the speaker's own life, set against a pride of lions.

stichs.en: I will thank You in a great assembly;
among a mighty people I will praise You.

verses.summary: The second vow of praise, and the payment is offered in advance. Not private thanks, but thanks said in front of a crowd.

stichs.en: Let my enemies not rejoice over me falsely,
let those who hate me without cause not wink the eye.

verses.summary: The petition resumes with the key phrase again: hatred without cause. Winking the eye is the gesture of a conspiracy that has already agreed on its story.

stichs.en: For they do not speak peace,
and against the quiet of the land they devise words of deceit.

verses.summary: The charge is specified. They are not loud, they are quiet and busy, and their targets are the people who want no part of any of it.

stichs.en: They opened their mouth wide against me;
they said: Aha, aha, our eye has seen it.

verses.summary: The mouth finally opens. Aha twice, and then the sentence that seals a false verdict: we saw it ourselves.

stichs.en: You have seen, LORD; do not be silent.
My Lord, do not be far from me.

verses.summary: The answer to verse 21, word for word. They say our eye has seen; the reply is You have seen. Then two negative petitions, do not stay silent and do not stay far.

stichs.en: Rouse Yourself and awake to my judgment,
my God and my Lord, to my case.

verses.summary: Both verbs are wake-up words. The complaint is not that God is absent but that He has not yet moved, and the vocabulary is entirely courtroom.

stichs.en: Judge me according to Your righteousness, LORD my God,
and let them not rejoice over me.

verses.summary: What is requested is not mercy but justice, measured by God's own righteousness. The second half repeats the opening of verse 19 almost exactly.

stichs.en: Let them not say in their heart: Aha, just what we wanted;
let them not say: We have swallowed him.

verses.summary: What the speaker fears here is not the blow but the sentence spoken over it. Two quotations, one whispered inside the heart and one said out loud.

stichs.en: Let those who rejoice at my harm be shamed and disgraced together;
let those who magnify themselves against me be clothed in shame and humiliation.

verses.summary: The last curse, tighter than the first: shame is now something worn. The two verbs of verse 4 come back, which closes the loop.

stichs.en: Let those who delight in my vindication shout for joy and be glad,
and let them say continually: The LORD be magnified,
who delights in the peace of His servant.

verses.summary: The mirror image of verse 26. The same verb of rejoicing, handed to the other side, and the psalm's last demand turns out to be peace for a servant rather than ruin for an enemy.

stichs.en: And my tongue will utter Your righteousness,
Your praise all the day.

verses.summary: The vow is made permanent. My tongue answers the wide mouths of verse 21, and all the day answers the how long of verse 17.

pardes.body: Three rounds, each with the same shape: a complaint, a petition against the attackers, then a vow to praise in public. They close at verses 9 and 10, at verse 18, and at verses 27 and 28. The vocabulary is mixed deliberately. Verses 1 to 3 are military, with shield, buckler and spear, and from verse 11 the setting is a trial: witnesses of violence, judge me, my case, my judgment. The verb at {{1.1}} is the legal one, to conduct a lawsuit, and {{1.4}} is built from the same root, so the psalm is already inside the courtroom before any weapon is named.

Three difficulties, all in the middle section. {{16.2}} is a rare word usually taken as a cake or a round loaf, which would make the line mockers who perform for their food, parasites at a table; the reading is not secure and translations differ. {{15.5}} is equally uncertain: smitten ones, smiters, or people the speaker does not know, and the ancient versions divide. The third is not a rare word but a real ambiguity: {{13.10}} says the prayer returns upon my bosom, which can mean the prayer came back unanswered, or that a prayer said for someone else comes home to the one who said it. Both readings are old and both are still printed.

The heading puts the psalm in David's mouth, and verses 13 and 14 are commonly read against the Saul chapters of Samuel: the man being hunted is the one who wore sackcloth and fasted when his hunters were ill, and who twice had Saul within reach and did not strike. Read that way the psalm is less a request for revenge than a demand that the record be entered. The line at {{10.1}}, all my bones, is the verse people reach for when they explain why the whole body moves during prayer, on the argument that praise is not the tongue's work alone. And {{7.1}}, without cause, is the phrase that becomes the standard name for hatred with no reason behind it, the failing the tradition blames for the loss of the Second Temple.

The angel of the LORD appears twice, at {{5.4}} and again in the following verse, once in front of the enemy driving and once behind pursuing. The mystical reading takes the pair as two faces of a single measure, judgement that pushes away and judgement that follows, and sets it beside the same figure in the neighbouring psalm, who encamps around those who fear Him. The other line read this way is {{13.10}}: a prayer poured out for someone who will later hunt you does not vanish when it goes unanswered, it returns to the chest it came from and does its work there. On that reading the harshest verses of the psalm and its strangest act of kindness are one movement seen from opposite ends.
